displayQuote: Strong people always have strong weaknesses too

meta.title: Who really said "Strong people always have strong weaknesses too"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Drucker wrote it: The Effective Executive (Harper & Row, 1967), ch. 4, p. 72. Reprints dropped the final 'too'; a 1989 book recast it as Attila the Hun.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Strong people always have strong weaknesses too'?
meta.ogDescription: Drucker really wrote it — The Effective Executive, 1967, page 72, verified against the first edition. The trimmed version and the Attila variant came later.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Drucker wrote it in The Effective Executive (Harper & Row, New York, 1967), in chapter 4, “Making Strength Productive,” on page 72. Quote Investigator verified that page against a hardcopy of the first edition, and the sentence sits inside Drucker’s argument against hiring “well-rounded” people.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually appears
source.excerpt: The idea that there are “well-rounded” people, people who have only strengths and no weaknesses . . . is a prescription for mediocrity if not for incompetence. Strong people always have strong weaknesses too. Where there are peaks, there are valleys.
trail: 1905 — the oxymoron is already in print. Edmund Downey’s Twenty Years Ago, a memoir of literary London, calls the journalist John Augustus O’Shea’s habit of introducing people under false names one of his “strong weaknesses” (full text ↗).

1967 — Drucker publishes the sentence in The Effective Executive, chapter 4, “Making Strength Productive,” page 72; Quote Investigator verified the page against a hardcopy (Quote Investigator ↗). The Harper & Row first edition ↗ lists that chapter.

1976 — John J. Tarrant’s Drucker biography ↗ (Cahners Books) reprints the saying in an appendix of Drucker one-liners — without the final “too.” Paul Dickson’s The Official Rules does the same in 1978.

1989 — Wess Roberts recasts it as “Strong chieftains always have strong weaknesses” in Leadership Secrets of Attila the Hun, in a chapter presenting the lines as Attila’s own thoughts. Quote Investigator concludes Roberts crafted the variant after Drucker’s remark was already circulating (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The ellipsis marks words omitted from the middle of Drucker’s first sentence in Quote Investigator’s transcription of page 72.

author.name: Peter Drucker
author.heading: About Peter Drucker
author.metaLine: 1909–2005 · Austrian-born American management consultant, educator and author
author.bio: Peter F. Drucker was an Austrian-born American management consultant, educator and author — more than anyone, the writer who turned management into a subject you could study. The Practice of Management (1954) and The Effective Executive (1967) remain his best-known books. His talent for compressing a whole argument into one blunt sentence is also why so many lines, genuine and invented, end up with his name attached.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: No serious source takes this line away from Drucker. What drifts is the wording — and one 1989 bestseller that handed a version of it to a fifth-century warlord.

items.who: “Strong people always have strong weaknesses” — without the “too”
items.why: John J. Tarrant’s 1976 Drucker biography ↗ and Paul Dickson’s 1978 The Official Rules both print the saying without Drucker’s final word. The clipped form stuck: the reader who brought the question to Quote Investigator ↗ had it as “Strong people have strong weaknesses.”

Wess Roberts’s Leadership Secrets of Attila the Hun (1989) prints “Strong chieftains always have strong weaknesses” in a chapter of ‘Attilaisms — Selected Thoughts of Attila.’ Quote Investigator ↗ concludes Roberts crafted the variant after Drucker’s remark was already in circulation — a modern author’s line dressed as an ancient one.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Drucker’s, and the full form has four beats, not three: “Strong people always have strong weaknesses too.” — The Effective Executive (Harper & Row, 1967), chapter 4, page 72, verified against a hardcopy by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: Drucker meant this as an argument, not an aphorism. The chapter it sits in, “Making Strength Productive,” is about how to staff an organisation, and his claim is that hiring to avoid weakness quietly selects for people with no sharp edges at all. Chasing the flawless candidate, he wrote, is “a prescription for mediocrity if not for incompetence.”

He set the point up with a story: Lincoln, told that General Grant drank too much, was supposed to have asked what brand, so he could send a barrel to his other generals. Quote Investigator — which located the Drucker page — treats that Lincoln whiskey line itself as legend, which is a useful reminder that a good anecdote and a documented quotation are not the same thing.
detailsBody: Not the phrase itself. Quote Investigator points to a 1905 memoir of literary London, Edmund Downey’s Twenty Years Ago, which describes the journalist John Augustus O’Shea’s taste for practical jokes as one of his “strong weaknesses.” The scanned page bears that out. What Drucker added was the turn from a wry description of one man into a general rule about people who get things done.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces "Strong people always have strong weaknesses too" to Peter F. Drucker, The Effective Executive, Chapter 4 'Making Strength Productive', Quote Page 72, Harper & Row, New York, 1967 (Verified with hardcopy); quotes the surrounding passage ending 'Where there are peaks, there are valleys'; documents the 1905 Downey 'strong weaknesses' precursor (p. 90), the 1974/75 Bump, 1976 Tarrant (p. 258, Cahners Books) and 1978 Dickson (p. 40) reprints, and the 1989 Wess Roberts variant 'Strong chieftains always have strong weaknesses' (Leadership Secrets of Attila the Hun, chapter 'Attilaisms: Selected Thoughts of Attila', p. 104); concludes Drucker deserves credit and Roberts crafted the variant afterwards; and calls the Lincoln/Grant whiskey-barrel line a legend.

Internet Archive catalog record for The Effective Executive by Peter F. Drucker (1909-2005), publisher Harper & Row, New York, 1967, whose listed contents include a chapter 'Making strength productive'.

Edmund Downey's Twenty Years Ago (1905) contains the passage: 'A trick of introducing people under wrong names was one of O'Shea's "strong weaknesses," and, as a rule, he succeeded in "selling" his acquaintances' — appearing immediately before the running head 'Further Chronicles of Catherine Street. 91', i.e. on page 90, matching Quote Investigator's citation.

A 2017 edition of The Effective Executive: The Definitive Guide to Getting the Right Things Done is published by HarperBusiness, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers, New York.
Peter Drucker lived 19 November 1909 to 11 November 2005, was an Austrian-born American management consultant, educator and author, and The Effective Executive (1967) appears in his bibliography.

Wikiquote's Peter Drucker page carries a 'Misattributed' section (listing 'Culture eats strategy for breakfast') and does not include 'Strong people always have strong weaknesses too' in either its sourced quotations or its misattributed list.
